speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Can you describe how the swelling and pain in your right ring finger started, and have you noticed any recent injuries or insect bites in that area?

speaker: Patient
text: 22-year-old male. The patient reports that the pain and swelling in his right ring finger began 2 days ago while playing football. He recalls his finger got caught in the jersey of another player, who then pulled away forcefully.

speaker: Doctor
text: That sounds like a significant mechanism of injury, potentially involving a fracture or a severe ligament tear. On a scale of 1 to 10, how would you rate your current pain level, and are you able to fully bend or straighten the finger?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Progressive swelling and pain in the right ring finger. I also have Inability to flex the right ring finger at the distal interphalangeal joint when making a fist, Pain at the distal interphalangeal joint, Extended right ring finger in resting position.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint combined with the mechanism of injury strongly suggests a "Jersey Finger," which is an avulsion of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon. To confirm this, I need to visualize the tendon's integrity and rule out a bony avulsion.

text: RESULTS: X-ray of the Right Hand: No bone fractures or dislocations visible. Soft tissue swelling noted around the distal interphalangeal joint of the right ring finger. Ultrasound_hand: NORMAL READINGS

speaker: Doctor
text:
The normal ultrasound is unusual for a Jersey Finger, which typically shows tendon retraction. Let me physically examine the finger to see if there is a gap in the tendon at the DIP joint or if the tendon slips proximally when you attempt to flex.

text: Thank you for that history. Have you noticed any numbness or tingling in the finger, and does the pain radiate up your arm or stay localized to the fingertip?

speaker: Doctor
text:
The absence of numbness rules out major nerve involvement, and the normal ultrasound makes a simple tendon rupture less likely if the tendon is intact. Since the patient cannot actively flex the DIP joint but has no fracture, this could be a tendon injury missed by ultrasound or a mechanical block.
